items.summary_html:
Last week ScaleDown launched Constrained Decoding Models (CDMs). The launch post got about 1.8M views. The pitch is simple: most production LLM calls don't need prose. They need a label, a field, or a short summary. So instead of a general model writing an answer token by token, each CDM does one job, reads your input once, and returns a typed result. Pricing is $0.05 per million input tokens (OpenRouter lists $0.04 with a 20% promo), and output is free.

The launch post made big claims: "200x faster, 467x cheaper than frontier LLM APIs" and "77.2% on DecisionBench". A thread from Bitroot pushed back the next day. Their point was that the 467x has no stated baseline, DecisionBench has no public source, and nobody should trust a classifier result without a few hundred labelled examples and confidence intervals. That's a fair critique, so I built the test around it.

Here's what I ran, what held up, and what didn't.

The setup

I'm a Lead SWE, so I tested this the way I'd vet any vendor before routing production traffic to it: public labelled data, the same prompts for every engine, and raw results saved to disk.

  • Classify: 300 CLINC150 test utterances (10 intents plus 50 out-of-scope) and 110 Bitext customer-support tickets across 11 categories.
  • Extract: 50 SROIE receipts (company, date, address, total) and 30 LinkedIn job posts (company, top of pay range, and work type as an enum).
  • Summarize: 6 QMSum meeting transcripts (4k to 9k tokens), 2 long ones (31k tokens), and one 369k-token stress doc.
  • Baseline: Qwen3 1.7B running locally on Ollama (8-core CPU, no GPU), with the same instructions and JSON-schema-constrained output. I didn't have a frontier API key on this box, so for frontier models I did list-price math from the official pricing pages (checked 22 Oct 2026).

Everything goes through one OpenAI-compatible base URL. Classify also has a Jev-compatible Decisions endpoint, which is the one I used most:

import httpx, os
r = httpx.post(
    "https://api.scaledown.xyz/v1/scaledown",
    headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["SCALEDOWN_API_KEY"]},
    json={
        "state": {"text": "how do I reset my pin"},
        "questions": {"intent": {"type": "choice", "criteria": {
            "pin_change": "wants to change or reset their PIN",
            "balance": "asks for an account balance",
            "oos": "none of the above / out of scope",
        }}},
    },
)
print(r.json()["answers"]["intent"])
# {'type': 'choice', 'choice': 'pin_change', 'confidence': 0.979, ...}

Each response includes a usage.cost field. Mine always worked out to exactly $0.05 per million billed input tokens.

Classify: the strongest result 
CLINC150 (n=300, 10 intents + out-of-scope)   accuracy   95% CI          OOS recall
ScaleDown Decisions (classify-1)              97.3%      94.8 - 98.6%    98%
ScaleDown /classify (rubrics)                 96.7%      94.0 - 98.2%    100%
Qwen3 1.7B local                              90.7%      86.8 - 93.5%    86%

Bitext support tickets (n=110, 11 categories)
ScaleDown Decisions                           92.7%      86.3 - 96.3%
ScaleDown /classify                           90.9%      84.1 - 95.0%
Qwen3 1.7B local                              62.7%      53.4 - 71.2%

The confidence intervals don't overlap with the small local model on either set. On CLINC150 the out-of-scope handling impressed me most. It correctly rejected 49 of 50 out-of-scope queries, and only 6 in-scope queries were wrongly pushed to "oos". That's the failure that hurts in a real router.

I didn't need any prompt engineering. I wrote one plain-English line per label, and that was it.

Latency, sequential, measured from a cloud box in India: p50 162 ms, p95 397 ms for Decisions, and p50 134 ms for /classify with reasoning: false. The ticket set had a longer tail (p95 about 1.0 s).

Extract: good spans, and the misses are interesting

Extract takes a standard response_format JSON schema. Each property's description is the search criteria, and every value comes back with a confidence score and character offsets into your input.

schema = {"type": "object", "properties": {
    "company":    {"type": "string", "description": "the hiring company's name"},
    "max_salary": {"type": "string", "description": "the top of the stated salary or pay range"},
    "work_type":  {"type": "string", "enum": ["Full-time", "Contract", "Part-time"],
                   "description": "employment type"},
}}
client.chat.completions.create(
    model="extract",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": job_post}],
    response_format={"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": "job", "schema": schema}},
    extra_body={"top_n": 1, "context_chars": 0},
)

                        field acc   valid JSON   spans verbatim   p50 latency
Receipts (50 SROIE)
  ScaleDown Extract     89.5%       100%         100%             1.43 s
  Qwen3 1.7B local      89.5%       100%         94%              3.55 s
Job posts (30)
  ScaleDown Extract     90.0%       100%         n/a              0.60 s
  Qwen3 1.7B local      81.1%       100%         n/a              2.76 s

Per field on receipts, ScaleDown got 100% of totals right, compared with 78% for the local model. Totals are the field you actually care about. It was weaker on company names (80% vs 88%).

Every span ScaleDown returned appeared verbatim in the source text. The citations aren't decoration. You can highlight exactly where a value came from, which is what Bitroot said to check.

I read every miss, and most were judgment calls rather than hallucinations:

  • The SROIE gold "date" often includes the time (21 MAR 2018 17:59). ScaleDown returned just the date.
  • It returned KING'S CONFECTIONERY S/B without the registration number the label includes.
  • On job posts it sometimes returned the parent company instead of the brand (ManpowerGroup for an Experis post, HCA Healthcare for MountainView Hospital).
  • One real error: on one bakery delivery receipt it picked the buyer's name and address instead of the seller's. That template appeared 4 times in my random sample, so it cost 8 field points on its own.

Valid JSON was 100% on both engines, but that's partly because I constrained the local model's output with a schema. The bigger difference is that ScaleDown hands back offsets and a confidence score with no extra work.

Summarize: fast and faithful, but watch the query focus

For summaries I passed the QMSum query as the system instruction and the transcript as the user message.

QMSum meetings, 4k-9k tokens (n=6)   p50       p95       ROUGE-L   summaries w/ invented facts
ScaleDown Summarize                  0.65 s    0.89 s    0.230     0 of 6
Qwen3 1.7B local (CPU)               24.3 s    34.1 s    0.201     2 of 6

I checked every number and name in each summary against the transcript. ScaleDown's held up, including the details: a 2.39 average rating, the drop from 15 to 12.50 euros, and the 50 million euro profit target were all there in the source. The local model said one rating used "1 to 5" when the meeting used a seven-point scale. It also called an over-budget prototype "reasonably priced".

Two weaknesses showed up:

  • Query focus. In one meeting it summarised the presentation instead of answering "what did the PM question". On both 31k-token transcripts it summarised an adjacent part of the meeting rather than the exact question. It's a summarizer first and a QA model second.
  • The 1M-context claim. I sent a 369k-token document made of 12 concatenated meetings and asked for one or two sentences per meeting. It accepted the input and returned in 14.2 s. The summary, though, covered only one of the two distinct meeting series in the document and skipped the other entirely. So it can ingest that much, but don't rely on coverage at that length.
Is it really 200x faster?

Not against anything I could measure, and not according to ScaleDown's own docs.

Against a 1.7B model on my CPU, it was 1.8x faster for short classification, 2.5 to 4.6x for extraction, and about 37x for 6k-token summaries, where CPU prompt processing dominates. A local CPU model isn't a frontier API, though. ScaleDown's own head-to-head benchmark page reports 2.2x to 13.9x faster than each provider's lineup average (2.4x vs OpenAI, 3.8x vs Anthropic). That's a solid speedup, but it's an order of magnitude below the launch post's 200x. I couldn't find what "200x" was measured against.

Is it really 467x cheaper?

The price is real. Every call billed exactly $0.05 per million input tokens, and output was free. The ratio, though, depends entirely on the baseline, and there's a catch: ScaleDown bills more input tokens than your raw prompt. Label criteria, schemas and internal prompts are counted. My classify calls billed about 481 tokens, while the same task as a plain LLM prompt was 172 tokens. Extract calls billed about 1,380 tokens against 571.

Here's the cost per 1,000 calls at list price, using my measured token counts and leaving out reasoning tokens:

                         classify   extract   summarize (6k tok)
ScaleDown CDM            $0.024     $0.069    $0.317
gpt-5-nano               $0.012     $0.057    $0.333     (0.5x - 1.0x)
gpt-5.4-nano             $0.044     $0.204    $1.300     (1.8x - 4.1x)
gpt-5.4-mini             $0.163     $0.752    $4.860     (6.8x - 15x)
Claude Haiku 4.5         $0.210     $0.931    $6.394     (8.7x - 20x)
Claude Sonnet 4.6        $0.631     $2.793    $19.18     (26x - 61x)
gpt-5.5                  $1.089     $5.015    $32.40     (45x - 102x)
Claude Fable 5           $2.102     $9.311    $63.94     (87x - 202x)

So against the cheapest small models, ScaleDown costs about the same, and on short classification gpt-5-nano is actually half the price. Against flagship models it's 45x to 200x cheaper. You only reach 467x if the frontier model also spends a few hundred reasoning tokens per call. For example, gpt-5.5 classifying with 500 reasoning tokens works out to roughly 670x. That's realistic for a reasoning model doing routing, but it isn't stated anywhere in the launch post. ScaleDown's own docs are more modest: 89x cheaper than the OpenAI average and 161x cheaper than the Anthropic average.

The /classify endpoint accepts up to 50 chunks per request and bills the label set once. If you classify at volume, that removes most of the token overhead I measured.

Limitations: I didn't benchmark Compress or concurrent load this round; my free credits ran out after ~1M input tokens, since the 50M free tokens were a launch-window promo. After that I got 402 Insufficient credits, so budget for a top-up before you run a real eval.

What Bitroot got right

The skeptic thread was right on every point I could check:

  • 467x has no stated baseline. I can reproduce it only by assuming an expensive reasoning model.
  • I still found no public source for DecisionBench's 77.2%.
  • Price is the easy part to verify, and it checks out.

Their main advice was to build a test set of 300+ labelled examples and report intervals, and that advice is what made this test worth anything. With n=300, the gap between 97% and 91% is real. With n=30 it wouldn't be.

My take

I'd route classification traffic to ScaleDown today. It was the most accurate engine I tested, with clean out-of-scope handling, sub-200 ms p50 latency, and no prompt tuning. Extract is a strong default when you need provenance, because every value comes with an offset you can highlight. Summarize is fast and didn't invent facts in my sample, but test its query focus on your own data, and don't trust its coverage of 300k+ token inputs.

The marketing ratios are a different story. If you already run gpt-5-nano, you won't save much. If you run flagship or reasoning models for routing and extraction, the savings are large and real.

Test it on your own data. A few hundred labelled examples will tell you more than any launch post, mine included.

items.title: Ledger Sloth: a bank statement reader that never phones home
items.summary: Submitted to the DEV × MLH Hacktoberfest Week 3 challenge ("Slow and Steady"), for the Best Use of TabPFN and Best Use of Gemma featured categories. The hook — the chore everyone dreads, monthly Once a month, the statement lands. A few hundred lines of bank-speak — ACH D- ZERODHA BROKING SIP , UPI-SWIGGY-BANGALORE , a ₹999 charge from a tool you trialled in August and forgot by September. Somewhere in there is the answer to "where did the money go?", and getting it out means an evening with a spreadsheet, or uploading the most revealing document you own to a website and hoping. Ledger Sloth is the lazy way out — appropriately, for International Sloth Day. Point it at the statement CSV your bank already gives you: npx tsx src/index.ts report statement.csv It reads every transaction, categorizes it, and writes a month-in-review: where the money went, what changed versus last month, which subscriptions renewed silently, which charges look wrong — plus a forecast of next month's spending per category, and a categorized CSV for your records. It runs at CPU speed, on your machine, and it is in no hurry. Neither are you. That's the point. What it does One command takes one statement CSV (HDFC layout first; ICICI and SBI variants and a generic signed-amount shape too) and produces three files in an output folder: report.md , a self-contained report.html , and categorized.csv — every transaction with its category, ready for a spreadsheet or an accountant. In between, every row is parsed and normalized; categorized by a local correction memory, then deterministic rules, then Gemma; aggregated into per-category totals and month-over-month deltas; scored by TabPFN, which forecasts next month per category and scores every debit against what it expected that charge to be; and written up by Gemma into a plain-English month-in-review whose every rupee figure is mechanically checked against the computed aggregates before it is allowed into the report. Categorizes every transaction (memory → rules → Gemma — see below). Flags anomalous charges with reasons built from your own history. Forecasts next month's per-category spend with TabPFN — and tells you, honestly, whether that forecast beat the naive guess (see "The honest benchmark"). Learns your corrections locally: correct "NOTION LABS" Subscriptions writes one line to a JSON file on your disk, and that merchant is yours forever — no retraining, no account, no sync. Architecture — two models, never in the room together statement.csv │ ▼ parse ──► categorize ──► aggregate ──► TabPFN worker ──► narrate ──► render (TS) memory → rules (pure TS) (Python, spawned (Gemma — report.md → Gemma (Ollama) once, one JSON figures report.html job, then exits) checked) categorized.csv The pipeline is a straight line, and its shape is the privacy story: Parse. A hand-rolled RFC-4180 reader maps the statement's columns into typed transactions. Unrecognized layouts fail loudly, listing the headers found — never a silent guess. Categorize, deterministic first. A local correction memory (your teachings, in a JSON file you can read and edit) and an ordered merchant-rule table categorize everything they know — instantly, offline, explainably. Categorize, Gemma for the long tail. Whatever is left goes, in batches, to Gemma 3 4B running locally via Ollama . Replies are validated — exact length, categories checked against the fixed list — before a single row is mapped; anything invalid degrades to Other and is counted, in the open, in the run metrics. The stage's last request unloads the model. Aggregate. Totals, month-over-month deltas, top merchants, medians — pure functions, unit-tested against hand-computed values. Forecast + anomaly scoring with TabPFN. A separate Python process is spawned once, handed one JSON job (forecast, honest benchmark, expected amounts), and exits — so PyTorch and Gemma are never resident at the same time . On a small machine that isn't an optimization; it's the difference between running and swapping to death. On the 7.7 GB box this was built on, Gemma peaks at 3,773 MB and TabPFN at 3,933 MB — comfortable one at a time, impossible together. Narrate. Gemma returns for one call whose prompt contains only the aggregates. Every ₹-figure it writes is then checked against those aggregates — it must exist, be written in well-formed digit grouping, and be used in the right scope (see "Grounding the narrator"). Fail, and the narrative is retried once, then replaced by a templated summary — and the report says so, in the report. The model proposes; the code disposes. Render. report.md , a self-contained report.html (zero external references — the offline claim holds even when you view the report), and categorized.csv , byte-identical across runs — I verified that across four full runs, including one with no network at all. Why open — bank statements are data you never upload There is a short list of documents that describe a life almost completely: a month of bank transactions is on it. Salary, rent, medicines, the 2 a.m. food orders, the loan you're quiet about — it's all there, timestamped. Tools that analyze statements almost always ask you to upload that document to someone else's server, where "analysis" means it joins a database you can't see, under a privacy policy you'll never read. Open-weight models change who can build this tool. Gemma 3 (open-weight under the Gemma Terms of Use) runs on the laptop that already holds the statement. TabPFN — a foundation model for tabular data — runs the forecast locally after a one-time weights download: the TabPFN-3.5 weights are open-weight under Prior Labs' non-commercial TABPFN-3-5 License v1.0, and the tabpfn package code itself is Apache 2.0. Nothing in Ledger Sloth's design requires a server, an account, or a network: after setup, the only HTTP it makes is to localhost . That's not a privacy policy ; it's an architecture. You don't have to trust it — you can watch it work with the Wi-Fi off. I did: a full run inside a network namespace with no egress route at all (a curl to the outside fails) completed with the identical benchmark verdict and identical output. And the local part compounds. Your corrections live in a JSON file on your disk, making next month's run better without a single byte leaving the machine. The cost structure is a consequence of the openness too: after the one-time downloads, a run costs ₹0 — no API bill scales with your bank history. Open weights make this possible , not just cheaper: a hosted API version of Ledger Sloth would be a different, worse product wearing the same name. The honest benchmark TabPFN's forecast is only worth having if it beats the forecast a spreadsheet makes for free: next month = this month . So Ledger Sloth benchmarks itself on a held-out month — same model, same features, cutoff moved — and prints the verdict either way. On the fixture statement (four months, Jun–Sep 2026; Sep held out; 12 spend categories), the verdict is: The naive baseline won — naive MAE ₹2,558.75 vs TabPFN MAE ₹2,806.45. Why, honestly: this household is metronome-stable. Rent is ₹28,000 every month, investments ₹10,000, food within a few hundred rupees. Repeating last month scores zero error on five categories and under ₹200 on six more. The only row where either model was badly wrong was Shopping — September's actual (₹36,147) contains the planted anomaly, and both models missed it by ~₹30,000. One held-out month and 12 categories is a small sample, and the report says that too; this verdict describes this statement's benchmark, not TabPFN in general. What TabPFN's predictions looked like anyway: on the big steady categories they were genuinely close — rent ₹28,004.74 against an actual ₹28,000 (off by ₹4.74), food & dining ₹14,828.06 against ₹14,641 (off by ₹187), transport within ₹188. It lost on the small jumpy categories (utilities, entertainment), where it predicted rises that didn't happen, and on the anomaly row, where both models were equally blindsided. With three training months, "close but not closest" is the true result — so the forecast is the part of this tool I make the smallest claim for. Where TabPFN earned its place is the next section. The same rawness applies to the forecast itself: next month's Shopping forecast prints as ₹82,866.32, because the model trained on the anomaly month as-is. The report shows it unadjusted, with a note naming the flagged charge — rather than quietly cleaning the input to make the model look smarter. The anomaly that almost got away The anomaly detector scores each debit against a TabPFN model of expected amounts. The fixture plants one charge that must be caught: ₹32,999 at CROMA on 2026-09-14, in a Shopping history whose category median is ₹1,774. The flag rule is conservative — actual must exceed 2.5× the expected amount and the gap must exceed ₹1,000. The first working version expected ₹21,834 for that charge — a ratio of 1.51×. No flag. The detector missed the one charge it existed to catch, and the reason was a leak, not the model: the merchantMedian feature for a merchant that occurs exactly once is that charge's own amount . The feature contained the answer. Fix one: leave-one-out merchant medians — the median of the merchant's other debits, falling back to the category median. The expected amount barely moved: ₹20,294 (1.63×). Because the second leak was subtler: TabPFN is an in-context learner, and the scoring protocol fit on all debits and predicted the same rows — the CROMA row sat in its own training context, under a merchant key that occurs once, pulling its prediction toward itself. Fix two: the amounts job is now 5-fold cross-fitted inside the worker — every debit is predicted only by a model fit on the other folds. A charge is never scored by a model that saw it. Expected amount for CROMA: ₹1,938.50 — so ₹32,999 flags at ~17× expected, a gap of ~₹31,061 , with the reason printed in the report. It is the only flag on the fixture, which is also correct: nothing else in four months deserved one. An anomaly detector graded on its own homework will pass every exam and catch nothing; cross-fitting is what makes the flag mean something. Grounding the narrator The narrative is the one place a language model writes prose about your money, so it is the place the design trusts it least. Gemma sees only the aggregates JSON — never the statement — and every ₹-figure in its draft is extracted and checked before the draft is accepted. The first version checked only that figures exist in the aggregates. My adversarial QA pass caught why that's not enough: one draft wrote of Shopping "a significant increase of ₹52,740" — ₹52,740 is real, but it's Shopping's whole-period total; September's actual month-over-month change was +₹30,148. Right number, wrong scope, false sentence. Another run produced a correct total with mangled digit grouping ("₹11,1622"). Grounding is now three checks: a figure must exist in the payload, be written in well-formed grouping, and be used in its proper scope — whole-period figures only with whole-period framing. Failures get one sterner retry, then the deterministic template takes over, and the substitution is disclosed in the report body and the run metrics. On the final verification run before writing this post, both Gemma drafts failed on genuinely bad figures — an invented ₹52,747, per-category errors the model derived itself, a ×10 slip (₹11,20,000) — and the report shipped the template instead: plainer, correct, and labelled as a template. The trade-off is real and I'll state it: stricter grounding means more fallbacks, and a failed attempt costs another generation (that run's narrative stage took 347 s; the whole run 6 min 45 s against just under four minutes when a draft grounds first try). The report is never wrong. At worst, it's plainer. Numbers (all measured, none estimated) Measured on the build host: 2 vCPU · 7.7 GB RAM · CPU-only, no GPU (Ollama 0.40.6, tabpfn 9.2.0, torch 2.14.1+cpu, Python 3.12.3, Node 24). TabPFN spike: CPU-only torch installed in 84 s; tabpfn in 235 s; TabPFN-3.5 checkpoint 876 MB, downloaded once, offline after; a 200-row fit+predict took 38.7 s at 3,933 MB peak RSS. Gemma spike: model load 36.6 s; categorization at 6.64 tokens/s; narrative generation at 6.57 tokens/s (267 tokens in 57.6 s); peak RSS 3,773 MB; keep_alive: 0 unload verified (server RSS falls to 34 MB afterwards). Categorization: the deterministic layer (memory + rules) settled 249/249 rows (100%) of the fixture with zero leftovers — the fixture persona runs on 28 regular narration templates, and the post should be honest that the rules, not the model, carry this number. Gemma alone, verified live: 23/25 (92.0%) on a sample of real narrations, and 8/8 on synthetic merchants the rules had never seen (Zudio, Bikanervala, Dr Lal PathLabs, Kalyan Jewellers…). Accuracy vs ground truth on the full pipeline: 249/249 = 100.0% (the target was ≥85%). Source counts print in every report — on the fixture: memory 0 · rule 249 · Gemma 0 · Other 0. TabPFN on the fixture: one worker run does all three jobs — in the demo run, 57.9 s total (forecast fit 17.0 s, benchmark 2.3 s, amounts 37.1 s cross-fitted), scoring all 243 debits and forecasting exactly the 12 categories with history. A category with no history gets "no history — no forecast", never a fabricated ₹0. Full run: just under four minutes when the narrative grounds on the first attempt (233 s of stage time; the narrative stage alone was 169 s of it); 6 min 45 s on the run where both drafts failed grounding and the disclosed template took over. The categorized CSV came out byte-identical in both — and in the offline run. Install footprint: Python env 1,328.6 MiB + TabPFN-3.5 checkpoint 835.4 MiB + gemma3:4b 3.4 GB — about 5.5 GB of disk, once. Tests: 149 passing, covering the parser, rules, grounding checks, worker protocol, failure modes, and the byte-identical-output guarantee. Failure modes are features here Each of these was exercised end-to-end, not just unit-tested: TabPFN unavailable (no token, no weights): the report is still produced, with the forecast and anomaly sections replaced by an explicit "unavailable because…" note. Nothing silently dropped, nothing invented. A single month of data: the forecast section states that at least two months of history are needed and extrapolates nothing. Anomaly scoring still runs within the month — CROMA flags there too, at ~22× its expected amount. Ollama not running: the run fails fast with the exact fix command ( ollama serve ) and produces zero partial artifacts. Garbage or unrecognized CSV: a plain failure message — for unknown layouts, listing the headers found and the shapes Ledger Sloth can read. No artifacts, no guessing. Zero outbound calls: after the one-time setup downloads, a full run needs no network at all (verified with no egress route, above). What it doesn't do (yet) PDF statements — CSV exports only, for now. Bank connections or syncing — by design; you bring the file. Long histories: the benchmark above is three training months, and on short, stable histories the naive baseline is genuinely hard to beat. The forecast should get more useful with a year of statements; I haven't measured that, so I won't claim it. The narrative sometimes ships as the templated summary — by design, disclosed when it happens (see "Grounding the narrator"). Layouts beyond HDFC, ICICI, SBI and the generic signed-amount shape will fail loudly rather than parse creatively. items.summary_html:
Submitted to the DEV × MLH Hacktoberfest Week 3 challenge ("Slow and Steady"), for the Best Use of TabPFN and Best Use of Gemma featured categories.

The hook — the chore everyone dreads, monthly

Once a month, the statement lands. A few hundred lines of bank-speak — ACH D- ZERODHA BROKING SIP, UPI-SWIGGY-BANGALORE, a ₹999 charge from a tool you trialled in August and forgot by September. Somewhere in there is the answer to "where did the money go?", and getting it out means an evening with a spreadsheet, or uploading the most revealing document you own to a website and hoping.

Ledger Sloth is the lazy way out — appropriately, for International Sloth Day. Point it at the statement CSV your bank already gives you:

npx tsx src/index.ts report statement.csv

It reads every transaction, categorizes it, and writes a month-in-review: where the money went, what changed versus last month, which subscriptions renewed silently, which charges look wrong — plus a forecast of next month's spending per category, and a categorized CSV for your records. It runs at CPU speed, on your machine, and it is in no hurry. Neither are you. That's the point.

What it does

One command takes one statement CSV (HDFC layout first; ICICI and SBI variants and a generic signed-amount shape too) and produces three files in an output folder: report.md, a self-contained report.html, and categorized.csv — every transaction with its category, ready for a spreadsheet or an accountant. In between, every row is parsed and normalized; categorized by a local correction memory, then deterministic rules, then Gemma; aggregated into per-category totals and month-over-month deltas; scored by TabPFN, which forecasts next month per category and scores every debit against what it expected that charge to be; and written up by Gemma into a plain-English month-in-review whose every rupee figure is mechanically checked against the computed aggregates before it is allowed into the report.

  • Categorizes every transaction (memory → rules → Gemma — see below).
  • Flags anomalous charges with reasons built from your own history.
  • Forecasts next month's per-category spend with TabPFN — and tells you, honestly, whether that forecast beat the naive guess (see "The honest benchmark").
  • Learns your corrections locally: correct "NOTION LABS" Subscriptions writes one line to a JSON file on your disk, and that merchant is yours forever — no retraining, no account, no sync.
Architecture — two models, never in the room together 
statement.csv
     │
     ▼
 parse ──► categorize ──► aggregate ──► TabPFN worker ──► narrate ──► render
 (TS)      memory → rules   (pure TS)    (Python, spawned   (Gemma —    report.md
            → Gemma (Ollama)              once, one JSON     figures    report.html
                                          job, then exits)   checked)   categorized.csv

The pipeline is a straight line, and its shape is the privacy story:

  1. Parse. A hand-rolled RFC-4180 reader maps the statement's columns into typed transactions. Unrecognized layouts fail loudly, listing the headers found — never a silent guess.
  2. Categorize, deterministic first. A local correction memory (your teachings, in a JSON file you can read and edit) and an ordered merchant-rule table categorize everything they know — instantly, offline, explainably.
  3. Categorize, Gemma for the long tail. Whatever is left goes, in batches, to Gemma 3 4B running locally via Ollama. Replies are validated — exact length, categories checked against the fixed list — before a single row is mapped; anything invalid degrades to Other and is counted, in the open, in the run metrics. The stage's last request unloads the model.
  4. Aggregate. Totals, month-over-month deltas, top merchants, medians — pure functions, unit-tested against hand-computed values.
  5. Forecast + anomaly scoring with TabPFN. A separate Python process is spawned once, handed one JSON job (forecast, honest benchmark, expected amounts), and exits — so PyTorch and Gemma are never resident at the same time. On a small machine that isn't an optimization; it's the difference between running and swapping to death. On the 7.7 GB box this was built on, Gemma peaks at 3,773 MB and TabPFN at 3,933 MB — comfortable one at a time, impossible together.
  6. Narrate. Gemma returns for one call whose prompt contains only the aggregates. Every ₹-figure it writes is then checked against those aggregates — it must exist, be written in well-formed digit grouping, and be used in the right scope (see "Grounding the narrator"). Fail, and the narrative is retried once, then replaced by a templated summary — and the report says so, in the report. The model proposes; the code disposes.
  7. Render. report.md, a self-contained report.html (zero external references — the offline claim holds even when you view the report), and categorized.csv, byte-identical across runs — I verified that across four full runs, including one with no network at all.
Why open — bank statements are data you never upload

There is a short list of documents that describe a life almost completely: a month of bank transactions is on it. Salary, rent, medicines, the 2 a.m. food orders, the loan you're quiet about — it's all there, timestamped. Tools that analyze statements almost always ask you to upload that document to someone else's server, where "analysis" means it joins a database you can't see, under a privacy policy you'll never read.

Open-weight models change who can build this tool. Gemma 3 (open-weight under the Gemma Terms of Use) runs on the laptop that already holds the statement. TabPFN — a foundation model for tabular data — runs the forecast locally after a one-time weights download: the TabPFN-3.5 weights are open-weight under Prior Labs' non-commercial TABPFN-3-5 License v1.0, and the tabpfn package code itself is Apache 2.0. Nothing in Ledger Sloth's design requires a server, an account, or a network: after setup, the only HTTP it makes is to localhost. That's not a privacy policy; it's an architecture. You don't have to trust it — you can watch it work with the Wi-Fi off. I did: a full run inside a network namespace with no egress route at all (a curl to the outside fails) completed with the identical benchmark verdict and identical output.

And the local part compounds. Your corrections live in a JSON file on your disk, making next month's run better without a single byte leaving the machine. The cost structure is a consequence of the openness too: after the one-time downloads, a run costs ₹0 — no API bill scales with your bank history. Open weights make this possible, not just cheaper: a hosted API version of Ledger Sloth would be a different, worse product wearing the same name.

The honest benchmark

TabPFN's forecast is only worth having if it beats the forecast a spreadsheet makes for free: next month = this month. So Ledger Sloth benchmarks itself on a held-out month — same model, same features, cutoff moved — and prints the verdict either way.

On the fixture statement (four months, Jun–Sep 2026; Sep held out; 12 spend categories), the verdict is:

The naive baseline won — naive MAE ₹2,558.75 vs TabPFN MAE ₹2,806.45.

Why, honestly: this household is metronome-stable. Rent is ₹28,000 every month, investments ₹10,000, food within a few hundred rupees. Repeating last month scores zero error on five categories and under ₹200 on six more. The only row where either model was badly wrong was Shopping — September's actual (₹36,147) contains the planted anomaly, and both models missed it by ~₹30,000. One held-out month and 12 categories is a small sample, and the report says that too; this verdict describes this statement's benchmark, not TabPFN in general.

What TabPFN's predictions looked like anyway: on the big steady categories they were genuinely close — rent ₹28,004.74 against an actual ₹28,000 (off by ₹4.74), food & dining ₹14,828.06 against ₹14,641 (off by ₹187), transport within ₹188. It lost on the small jumpy categories (utilities, entertainment), where it predicted rises that didn't happen, and on the anomaly row, where both models were equally blindsided. With three training months, "close but not closest" is the true result — so the forecast is the part of this tool I make the smallest claim for. Where TabPFN earned its place is the next section.

The same rawness applies to the forecast itself: next month's Shopping forecast prints as ₹82,866.32, because the model trained on the anomaly month as-is. The report shows it unadjusted, with a note naming the flagged charge — rather than quietly cleaning the input to make the model look smarter.

The anomaly that almost got away

The anomaly detector scores each debit against a TabPFN model of expected amounts. The fixture plants one charge that must be caught: ₹32,999 at CROMA on 2026-09-14, in a Shopping history whose category median is ₹1,774. The flag rule is conservative — actual must exceed 2.5× the expected amount and the gap must exceed ₹1,000.

The first working version expected ₹21,834 for that charge — a ratio of 1.51×. No flag. The detector missed the one charge it existed to catch, and the reason was a leak, not the model: the merchantMedian feature for a merchant that occurs exactly once is that charge's own amount. The feature contained the answer.

Fix one: leave-one-out merchant medians — the median of the merchant's other debits, falling back to the category median. The expected amount barely moved: ₹20,294 (1.63×). Because the second leak was subtler: TabPFN is an in-context learner, and the scoring protocol fit on all debits and predicted the same rows — the CROMA row sat in its own training context, under a merchant key that occurs once, pulling its prediction toward itself.

Fix two: the amounts job is now 5-fold cross-fitted inside the worker — every debit is predicted only by a model fit on the other folds. A charge is never scored by a model that saw it. Expected amount for CROMA: ₹1,938.50 — so ₹32,999 flags at ~17× expected, a gap of ~₹31,061, with the reason printed in the report. It is the only flag on the fixture, which is also correct: nothing else in four months deserved one. An anomaly detector graded on its own homework will pass every exam and catch nothing; cross-fitting is what makes the flag mean something.

Grounding the narrator

The narrative is the one place a language model writes prose about your money, so it is the place the design trusts it least. Gemma sees only the aggregates JSON — never the statement — and every ₹-figure in its draft is extracted and checked before the draft is accepted. The first version checked only that figures exist in the aggregates. My adversarial QA pass caught why that's not enough: one draft wrote of Shopping "a significant increase of ₹52,740" — ₹52,740 is real, but it's Shopping's whole-period total; September's actual month-over-month change was +₹30,148. Right number, wrong scope, false sentence. Another run produced a correct total with mangled digit grouping ("₹11,1622").

Grounding is now three checks: a figure must exist in the payload, be written in well-formed grouping, and be used in its proper scope — whole-period figures only with whole-period framing. Failures get one sterner retry, then the deterministic template takes over, and the substitution is disclosed in the report body and the run metrics. On the final verification run before writing this post, both Gemma drafts failed on genuinely bad figures — an invented ₹52,747, per-category errors the model derived itself, a ×10 slip (₹11,20,000) — and the report shipped the template instead: plainer, correct, and labelled as a template. The trade-off is real and I'll state it: stricter grounding means more fallbacks, and a failed attempt costs another generation (that run's narrative stage took 347 s; the whole run 6 min 45 s against just under four minutes when a draft grounds first try). The report is never wrong. At worst, it's plainer.

Numbers (all measured, none estimated)

Measured on the build host: 2 vCPU · 7.7 GB RAM · CPU-only, no GPU (Ollama 0.40.6, tabpfn 9.2.0, torch 2.14.1+cpu, Python 3.12.3, Node 24).

  • TabPFN spike: CPU-only torch installed in 84 s; tabpfn in 235 s; TabPFN-3.5 checkpoint 876 MB, downloaded once, offline after; a 200-row fit+predict took 38.7 s at 3,933 MB peak RSS.
  • Gemma spike: model load 36.6 s; categorization at 6.64 tokens/s; narrative generation at 6.57 tokens/s (267 tokens in 57.6 s); peak RSS 3,773 MB; keep_alive: 0 unload verified (server RSS falls to 34 MB afterwards).
  • Categorization: the deterministic layer (memory + rules) settled 249/249 rows (100%) of the fixture with zero leftovers — the fixture persona runs on 28 regular narration templates, and the post should be honest that the rules, not the model, carry this number. Gemma alone, verified live: 23/25 (92.0%) on a sample of real narrations, and 8/8 on synthetic merchants the rules had never seen (Zudio, Bikanervala, Dr Lal PathLabs, Kalyan Jewellers…). Accuracy vs ground truth on the full pipeline: 249/249 = 100.0% (the target was ≥85%). Source counts print in every report — on the fixture: memory 0 · rule 249 · Gemma 0 · Other 0.
  • TabPFN on the fixture: one worker run does all three jobs — in the demo run, 57.9 s total (forecast fit 17.0 s, benchmark 2.3 s, amounts 37.1 s cross-fitted), scoring all 243 debits and forecasting exactly the 12 categories with history. A category with no history gets "no history — no forecast", never a fabricated ₹0.
  • Full run: just under four minutes when the narrative grounds on the first attempt (233 s of stage time; the narrative stage alone was 169 s of it); 6 min 45 s on the run where both drafts failed grounding and the disclosed template took over. The categorized CSV came out byte-identical in both — and in the offline run.
  • Install footprint: Python env 1,328.6 MiB + TabPFN-3.5 checkpoint 835.4 MiB + gemma3:4b 3.4 GB — about 5.5 GB of disk, once.
  • Tests: 149 passing, covering the parser, rules, grounding checks, worker protocol, failure modes, and the byte-identical-output guarantee.
Failure modes are features here

Each of these was exercised end-to-end, not just unit-tested:

  • TabPFN unavailable (no token, no weights): the report is still produced, with the forecast and anomaly sections replaced by an explicit "unavailable because…" note. Nothing silently dropped, nothing invented.
  • A single month of data: the forecast section states that at least two months of history are needed and extrapolates nothing. Anomaly scoring still runs within the month — CROMA flags there too, at ~22× its expected amount.
  • Ollama not running: the run fails fast with the exact fix command (ollama serve) and produces zero partial artifacts.
  • Garbage or unrecognized CSV: a plain failure message — for unknown layouts, listing the headers found and the shapes Ledger Sloth can read. No artifacts, no guessing.
  • Zero outbound calls: after the one-time setup downloads, a full run needs no network at all (verified with no egress route, above).
What it doesn't do (yet)
  • PDF statements — CSV exports only, for now.
  • Bank connections or syncing — by design; you bring the file.
  • Long histories: the benchmark above is three training months, and on short, stable histories the naive baseline is genuinely hard to beat. The forecast should get more useful with a year of statements; I haven't measured that, so I won't claim it.
  • The narrative sometimes ships as the templated summary — by design, disclosed when it happens (see "Grounding the narrator").
  • Layouts beyond HDFC, ICICI, SBI and the generic signed-amount shape will fail loudly rather than parse creatively.
Try it 
git clone https://github.com/pintu544/ledger-sloth.git
cd ledger-sloth
npm install

# Python sidecar: CPU-only torch FIRST (avoids the multi-GB CUDA build)
python3 -m venv python/.venv
python/.venv/bin/pip install torch==2.14.1 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
python/.venv/bin/pip install -r python/requirements.txt   # tabpfn==9.2.0

ollama pull gemma3:4b
# one-time: accept the TabPFN-3.5 license at platform.priorlabs.ai,
# copy the token from your account page, then:
export TABPFN_TOKEN=

ollama serve &   # if it isn't already running
npx tsx src/index.ts report fixtures/statement.csv

The demo statement is synthetic (a salaried persona, Jun–Sep 2026, one planted anomaly) with published ground truth, so every number in this post can be checked by hand. Slow, local, and in no hurry — that's the whole idea. 🦥

items.title: Give your AI agent SEC EDGAR data: a free remote MCP server for insider trades and XBRL financials
items.summary: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an AI client such as Claude, Cursor or VS Code call external tools through one common interface. This post walks through a free, MIT-licensed MCP server for U.S. SEC EDGAR data. It runs remotely, so there's nothing to install and no API key. I'll show how to connect it, three real calls with their actual output, how it works inside, and where it falls short. Endpoint (Streamable HTTP, no key): https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp Source: https://github.com/monriah-studio/sec-edgar-mcp-remote MCP Registry name: io.github.monriah-studio/sec-edgar-mcp Why EDGAR needs a wrapper EDGAR is one of the best free financial datasets around: every insider trade, 10-K, 8-K and XBRL financial fact that U.S. public companies file. It's also awkward to use, especially for an agent: The User-Agent rule. SEC's fair-access policy asks every client to send a declared User-Agent with a contact email and to stay under 10 requests per second. Requests that skip this get 403s. An LLM making fetches on its own won't know that. CIK lookup. Most endpoints want a 10-digit Central Index Key ( 0000320193 ), not a ticker ( AAPL ). You have to look it up in a roughly 1 MB company_tickers.json file first. Form 4 is XML. Insider trades come as one XML document per filing, full of transaction codes (P, S, A, M, F, G), derivative tables and footnotes. XBRL is messy. The companyconcept JSON repeats the same period across many filings and mixes 3-month, 9-month and 12-month durations. Getting "net income by fiscal year" out of it means filtering and de-duplicating. The server does all of this and returns compact JSON. The seven tools Tool What it returns get_insider_trades Form 4 transactions for a company or an insider, with buy/sell totals and a 10b5-1 flag get_market_insider_buys Open-market insider purchases across the market, grouped by company, with cluster-buy detection (2+ insiders) get_company_filings Latest 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K (with item numbers) and other filings, with document links get_company_snapshot Revenue, margins, net income, EPS, cash flow, balance sheet and YoY growth from XBRL get_company_concept Annual or quarterly history of any XBRL tag search_filings EDGAR full-text search with phrase, form and date filters resolve_company Ticker â†” CIK lookup Every tool takes a ticker or a CIK, and all of them are marked read-only. Connect a client Cursor : add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json (or .cursor/mcp.json in a project): { "mcpServers" : { "sec-edgar" : { "url" : "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp" } } } VS Code (Copilot agent mode): add this to .vscode/mcp.json : { "servers" : { "sec-edgar" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp" } } } Claude Desktop : on plans that support custom connectors, add the URL under Settings â†’ Connectors. You can also bridge it through claude_desktop_config.json with the mcp-remote package (needs Node.js): { "mcpServers" : { "sec-edgar" : { "command" : "npx" , "args" : [ "-y" , "mcp-remote" , "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp" ] } } } Claude Code : claude mcp add --transport http sec-edgar https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp Then try prompts like "Show NVIDIA's last insider sales and whether they were under 10b5-1 plans" or "Which companies had cluster insider buying this week?" Three real calls with curl The server is stateless, so you don't need an SDK to test it. Every request is a single JSON-RPC POST. Start with initialize : URL = https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp curl -s $URL \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1"}}}' { "result" :{ "protocolVersion" : "2025-06-18" , "capabilities" :{ "tools" :{}}, "serverInfo" :{ "name" : "sec-edgar-mcp" , "title" : "SEC EDGAR Insider Trades & Financials" , "version" : "1.0.0" }, ... }, "jsonrpc" : "2.0" , "id" : 1 } Each tool result comes back as JSON text in result.content[0].text . The outputs below are pretty-printed and trimmed ( ... ). I ran them on October 23, 2026, so your numbers will differ. 1. NVIDIA insider trades curl -s $URL -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_insider_trades","arguments":{"ticker_or_cik":"NVDA","filings":5,"max_rows":5}}}' { "company" : { "id" : "NVDA" , "cik" : "0001045810" , "ticker" : "NVDA" , "name" : "NVIDIA CORP" }, "filingsParsed" : 5 , "summary" : { "transactions" : 8 , "openMarketBuys" : 0 , "openMarketSells" : 5 , "sellShares" : 1396460 , "sellValueUsd" : 306933627.99 , "distinctInsiders" : 5 }, "returned" : 5 , "transactions" : [ { "date" : "2026-09-21" , "insider" : "Teter Timothy S." , "role" : "EVP, General Counsel and Sec" , "code" : "S" , "shares" : 12483 , "price" : 222.1932 , "valueUsd" : 2773637.72 , "ownedAfter" : 2705637 , "plan10b51" : true , "filed" : "2026-09-23" , "url" : "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000169684126000014/wk-form4_1790196985.xml" }, ... ] } On a cold cache, that call made 7 requests to SEC: the ticker map, the company's submissions index and five Form 4 XML files. The response header x-sec-requests: 7 reports the count. 2. Apple net income from XBRL curl -s $URL -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_company_concept","arguments":{"ticker_or_cik":"AAPL","concept":"NetIncomeLoss","period":"annual","limit":4}}}' { "company" : { "name" : "Apple Inc." , "cik" : "0000320193" }, "concept" : "us-gaap:NetIncomeLoss" , "label" : "Net Income (Loss) Attributable to Parent" , "unit" : "USD" , "period" : "annual" , "totalPeriods" : 19 , "values" : [ { "value" : 112010000000 , "start" : "2024-09-29" , "end" : "2025-09-27" , "fy" : 2025 , "form" : "10-K" , "filed" : "2025-10-31" }, { "value" : 93736000000 , "start" : "2023-10-01" , "end" : "2024-09-28" , "fy" : 2025 , "form" : "10-K" , "filed" : "2025-10-31" }, { "value" : 96995000000 , "start" : "2022-09-25" , "end" : "2023-09-30" , "fy" : 2025 , "form" : "10-K" , "filed" : "2025-10-31" }, ... ] } Look at fy . It's SEC's fiscal year of the filing that reported the value, not of the period, so the FY2024 figure shows fy: 2025 . Use start / end to know which period a value belongs to. 3. Cluster buys across the market curl -s $URL -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_market_insider_buys","arguments":{"days":7,"min_insiders":2,"limit":3}}}' { "window" : { "days" : 7 , "from" : "2026-10-17" , "to" : "2026-10-24" }, "dataUpdatedAt" : "2026-10-24T04:40:38.877Z" , "issuers" : 3 , "clusterBuys" : 3 , "results" : [ { "ticker" : "RAPP" , "issuer" : "Rapport Therapeutics, Inc." , "insiderCount" : 6 , "clusterBuy" : true , "totalValueUsd" : 1664824.35 , "totalShares" : 61694 , "avgPrice" : 26.9852 , "firstDate" : "2026-10-21" , "lastDate" : "2026-10-23" , "insiders" : [{ "name" : "Ignelzi Troy A." , "role" : "Chief Financial Officer" , "valueUsd" : 143550 }, ... ]}, { "ticker" : "CHCO" , "issuer" : "CITY HOLDING CO" , "insiderCount" : 4 , "totalValueUsd" : 68222.4 , ... }, { "ticker" : "RENT" , "issuer" : "Rent the Runway, Inc." , "insiderCount" : 3 , "totalValueUsd" : 6120515.95 , ... } ], "note" : "Open-market, non-derivative purchases only. Not investment advice." } This call made zero SEC requests because it reads from a pre-built store (more on that below). Dates are UTC, which is why the window ends on the 24th. How it works The whole thing is one Cloudflare Worker on the free plan: MCP transport. /mcp uses the official MCP TypeScript SDK's web-standard Streamable HTTP transport in stateless JSON mode. There are no sessions and no Durable Object per client. Each POST stands alone, and GET/DELETE return 405. Each tool maps to one REST endpoint, and a compact() function trims the REST JSON down to fewer fields and capped rows so it doesn't fill the model's context. The same Worker also serves that REST API ( /v1/... , documented in openapi.yaml ). SEC etiquette. Every request to SEC carries a declared User-Agent with a contact email. Requests are spaced at least 115 ms apart, and a global Durable Object rate limiter hands out time slots so that all Worker isolates together stay near 8.7 req/s, under SEC's 10 req/s ceiling. On 429/5xx the Worker backs off (honoring Retry-After ) and retries up to three times. A 403 gets one retry and then a clear error. Caching. Lookups go through three layers: isolate memory, then the Cloudflare Cache API, then KV for selected keys. TTLs follow how often the data changes. The ticker map and resolutions are cached for 24 h, parsed Form 4s for 30 days (filings don't change), submissions for 10 min, XBRL snapshots and concepts for 6 h, and full-text search for 15 min. Market-wide buys. A cron runs every 10 minutes. It queries EDGAR full-text search for new Form 4s, parses up to 40 per run, and keeps open-market purchases (code P, non-derivative) in a KV store. get_market_insider_buys groups that store by issuer. Ticker resolution. The ticker file is searched with a regex instead of JSON.parse , which keeps it inside the free plan's CPU budget. Limits and caveats Shallow per-call history. get_insider_trades parses at most 25 recent Form 4 filings per call (default 5). The free plan allows about 50 subrequests per invocation, so this isn't a tool for pulling ten years of history. Market scan coverage. The cluster-buy data covers at most 30 days and only starts from when the store was first populated. During a burst of filings the cron can fall behind. XBRL is only as clean as the filings. Companies choose different tags ( Revenues vs. RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax ), and some metrics will come back null. Check the tag field in the snapshot. Shared free endpoint. The public instance has no key and no SLA. Under heavy load you'll queue behind the global SEC limit or get a 503 asking you to retry. For anything important, deploy your own copy (the README covers it: a KV namespace, your own SEC_USER_AGENT , then wrangler deploy ). You can protect /mcp with MCP_API_KEYS . Not investment advice, not affiliated with the SEC. The data is public domain and comes straight from EDGAR. Interpreting it is up to you. A 10b5-1 sale means something very different from a discretionary open-market buy. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an AI client such as Claude, Cursor or VS Code call external tools through one common interface.

This post walks through a free, MIT-licensed MCP server for U.S. SEC EDGAR data. It runs remotely, so there's nothing to install and no API key. I'll show how to connect it, three real calls with their actual output, how it works inside, and where it falls short.

  • Endpoint (Streamable HTTP, no key): https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp
  • Source: https://github.com/monriah-studio/sec-edgar-mcp-remote
  • MCP Registry name: io.github.monriah-studio/sec-edgar-mcp
Why EDGAR needs a wrapper

EDGAR is one of the best free financial datasets around: every insider trade, 10-K, 8-K and XBRL financial fact that U.S. public companies file. It's also awkward to use, especially for an agent:

  1. The User-Agent rule. SEC's fair-access policy asks every client to send a declared User-Agent with a contact email and to stay under 10 requests per second. Requests that skip this get 403s. An LLM making fetches on its own won't know that.
  2. CIK lookup. Most endpoints want a 10-digit Central Index Key (0000320193), not a ticker (AAPL). You have to look it up in a roughly 1 MB company_tickers.json file first.
  3. Form 4 is XML. Insider trades come as one XML document per filing, full of transaction codes (P, S, A, M, F, G), derivative tables and footnotes.
  4. XBRL is messy. The companyconcept JSON repeats the same period across many filings and mixes 3-month, 9-month and 12-month durations. Getting "net income by fiscal year" out of it means filtering and de-duplicating.

The server does all of this and returns compact JSON.

The seven tools
Tool What it returns get_insider_trades Form 4 transactions for a company or an insider, with buy/sell totals and a 10b5-1 flag get_market_insider_buys Open-market insider purchases across the market, grouped by company, with cluster-buy detection (2+ insiders) get_company_filings Latest 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K (with item numbers) and other filings, with document links get_company_snapshot Revenue, margins, net income, EPS, cash flow, balance sheet and YoY growth from XBRL get_company_concept Annual or quarterly history of any XBRL tag search_filings EDGAR full-text search with phrase, form and date filters resolve_company Ticker â†” CIK lookup

Every tool takes a ticker or a CIK, and all of them are marked read-only.

Connect a client

Cursor: add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json (or .cursor/mcp.json in a project):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sec-edgar": {
      "url": "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp"
    }
  }
}

VS Code (Copilot agent mode): add this to .vscode/mcp.json:

{
  "servers": {
    "sec-edgar": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp"
    }
  }
}

Claude Desktop: on plans that support custom connectors, add the URL under Settings â†’ Connectors. You can also bridge it through claude_desktop_config.json with the mcp-remote package (needs Node.js):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sec-edgar": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http sec-edgar https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp

Then try prompts like "Show NVIDIA's last insider sales and whether they were under 10b5-1 plans" or "Which companies had cluster insider buying this week?"

Three real calls with curl

The server is stateless, so you don't need an SDK to test it. Every request is a single JSON-RPC POST. Start with initialize:

URL=https://sec-edgar-api.kidriahx.workers.dev/mcp
curl -s $URL \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1"}}}'

{"result":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{"tools":{}},"serverInfo":{"name":"sec-edgar-mcp","title":"SEC EDGAR Insider Trades & Financials","version":"1.0.0"}, ...},"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1}

Each tool result comes back as JSON text in result.content[0].text. The outputs below are pretty-printed and trimmed (...). I ran them on October 23, 2026, so your numbers will differ.

1. NVIDIA insider trades 
curl -s $URL -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_insider_trades","arguments":{"ticker_or_cik":"NVDA","filings":5,"max_rows":5}}}'

{
 "company": {"id": "NVDA", "cik": "0001045810", "ticker": "NVDA", "name": "NVIDIA CORP"},
 "filingsParsed": 5,
 "summary": {"transactions": 8, "openMarketBuys": 0, "openMarketSells": 5,
             "sellShares": 1396460, "sellValueUsd": 306933627.99, "distinctInsiders": 5},
 "returned": 5,
 "transactions": [
  {"date": "2026-09-21", "insider": "Teter Timothy S.", "role": "EVP, General Counsel and Sec",
   "code": "S", "shares": 12483, "price": 222.1932, "valueUsd": 2773637.72,
   "ownedAfter": 2705637, "plan10b51": true, "filed": "2026-09-23",
   "url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000169684126000014/wk-form4_1790196985.xml"},
  ...
 ]
}

On a cold cache, that call made 7 requests to SEC: the ticker map, the company's submissions index and five Form 4 XML files. The response header x-sec-requests: 7 reports the count.

2. Apple net income from XBRL 
curl -s $URL -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_company_concept","arguments":{"ticker_or_cik":"AAPL","concept":"NetIncomeLoss","period":"annual","limit":4}}}'

{
 "company": {"name": "Apple Inc.", "cik": "0000320193"},
 "concept": "us-gaap:NetIncomeLoss",
 "label": "Net Income (Loss) Attributable to Parent",
 "unit": "USD", "period": "annual", "totalPeriods": 19,
 "values": [
  {"value": 112010000000, "start": "2024-09-29", "end": "2025-09-27", "fy": 2025, "form": "10-K", "filed": "2025-10-31"},
  {"value": 93736000000,  "start": "2023-10-01", "end": "2024-09-28", "fy": 2025, "form": "10-K", "filed": "2025-10-31"},
  {"value": 96995000000,  "start": "2022-09-25", "end": "2023-09-30", "fy": 2025, "form": "10-K", "filed": "2025-10-31"},
  ...
 ]
}

Look at fy. It's SEC's fiscal year of the filing that reported the value, not of the period, so the FY2024 figure shows fy: 2025. Use start/end to know which period a value belongs to.

3. Cluster buys across the market 
curl -s $URL -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_market_insider_buys","arguments":{"days":7,"min_insiders":2,"limit":3}}}'

{
 "window": {"days": 7, "from": "2026-10-17", "to": "2026-10-24"},
 "dataUpdatedAt": "2026-10-24T04:40:38.877Z",
 "issuers": 3, "clusterBuys": 3,
 "results": [
  {"ticker": "RAPP", "issuer": "Rapport Therapeutics, Inc.", "insiderCount": 6, "clusterBuy": true,
   "totalValueUsd": 1664824.35, "totalShares": 61694, "avgPrice": 26.9852,
   "firstDate": "2026-10-21", "lastDate": "2026-10-23",
   "insiders": [{"name": "Ignelzi Troy A.", "role": "Chief Financial Officer", "valueUsd": 143550}, ...]},
  {"ticker": "CHCO", "issuer": "CITY HOLDING CO", "insiderCount": 4, "totalValueUsd": 68222.4, ...},
  {"ticker": "RENT", "issuer": "Rent the Runway, Inc.", "insiderCount": 3, "totalValueUsd": 6120515.95, ...}
 ],
 "note": "Open-market, non-derivative purchases only. Not investment advice."
}

This call made zero SEC requests because it reads from a pre-built store (more on that below). Dates are UTC, which is why the window ends on the 24th.

How it works

The whole thing is one Cloudflare Worker on the free plan:

  • MCP transport. /mcp uses the official MCP TypeScript SDK's web-standard Streamable HTTP transport in stateless JSON mode. There are no sessions and no Durable Object per client. Each POST stands alone, and GET/DELETE return 405. Each tool maps to one REST endpoint, and a compact() function trims the REST JSON down to fewer fields and capped rows so it doesn't fill the model's context. The same Worker also serves that REST API (/v1/..., documented in openapi.yaml).
  • SEC etiquette. Every request to SEC carries a declared User-Agent with a contact email. Requests are spaced at least 115 ms apart, and a global Durable Object rate limiter hands out time slots so that all Worker isolates together stay near 8.7 req/s, under SEC's 10 req/s ceiling. On 429/5xx the Worker backs off (honoring Retry-After) and retries up to three times. A 403 gets one retry and then a clear error.
  • Caching. Lookups go through three layers: isolate memory, then the Cloudflare Cache API, then KV for selected keys. TTLs follow how often the data changes. The ticker map and resolutions are cached for 24 h, parsed Form 4s for 30 days (filings don't change), submissions for 10 min, XBRL snapshots and concepts for 6 h, and full-text search for 15 min.
  • Market-wide buys. A cron runs every 10 minutes. It queries EDGAR full-text search for new Form 4s, parses up to 40 per run, and keeps open-market purchases (code P, non-derivative) in a KV store. get_market_insider_buys groups that store by issuer.
  • Ticker resolution. The ticker file is searched with a regex instead of JSON.parse, which keeps it inside the free plan's CPU budget.
Limits and caveats
  • Shallow per-call history. get_insider_trades parses at most 25 recent Form 4 filings per call (default 5). The free plan allows about 50 subrequests per invocation, so this isn't a tool for pulling ten years of history.
  • Market scan coverage. The cluster-buy data covers at most 30 days and only starts from when the store was first populated. During a burst of filings the cron can fall behind.
  • XBRL is only as clean as the filings. Companies choose different tags (Revenues vs. RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax), and some metrics will come back null. Check the tag field in the snapshot.
  • Shared free endpoint. The public instance has no key and no SLA. Under heavy load you'll queue behind the global SEC limit or get a 503 asking you to retry. For anything important, deploy your own copy (the README covers it: a KV namespace, your own SEC_USER_AGENT, then wrangler deploy). You can protect /mcp with MCP_API_KEYS.
  • Not investment advice, not affiliated with the SEC. The data is public domain and comes straight from EDGAR. Interpreting it is up to you. A 10b5-1 sale means something very different from a discretionary open-market buy.

  • For scheduled or bulk Form 4 pulls outside an agent loop, there's an Apify actor: https://apify.com/monriah-studio/sec-form4-insider-trades

import { Sandbox, Drive } from '@vercel/sandbox';

const drive = await Drive.getOrCreate({ name: 'agent-workspace' });
const sandbox = await Sandbox.create({
  mounts: { '/workspace': drive },
});

await sandbox.runCommand('git', ['clone', repoUrl, '/workspace/repo']);

items.title: The Silent Cascade: Why Workflow Success Blinds You to Hiring Stalls
items.summary: Your workflow just ran. Every metric looks perfect. Every node fired. The APIs returned 200. The logs are clean. The system declares victory and moves on. You check the dashboard—green across the board. Then, three days later, a candidate emails asking about interview timing. You pull up the records and find something strange: the round was marked "Completed," all three panelists were assigned, notifications were sent. But when you dig deeper—when you actually check—none of the panelists submitted scorecards. The interviews never happened. The round sat in limbo, looking successful to every automated system, while everyone waiting on it had no idea anything was wrong. This isn't a single failure. It's a cascade. And it happens because success at one layer of execution doesn't guarantee success at the next. Where the Blindness Starts Let's trace it from the beginning. A workflow succeeds when its steps execute. An n8n node fires, receives a 200, and logs completion. Every node in the chain behaves the same way. The workflow engine sees this as done. It reports success. This is true. But "the workflow executed" is not the same as "the workflow accomplished its goal." A notification can fire without being read. An assignment can log without being accepted. A request can return 200 without the human on the other end actually following through. Each local success hides the next breakdown point—and by the time you notice, the cascade has already compounded. This is where hiring rounds live. A candidate moves to Interview. The system logs it. Panelists get notified. From the workflow's perspective, every step succeeded. But from the hiring coordinator's perspective? Three days pass. No scorecards arrive. The candidate hasn't heard back. The round appears on track to every automated system while functionally stalling everywhere it matters. The workflow didn't fail. The workflow succeeded. But the outcome never landed. How Detection Blindness Compounds Here's the architecture of the problem: Layer 1: Execution success. The workflow runs. Every step completes. The system reports green. This is accurate—at the execution layer, nothing broke. Layer 2: Notification delivery. The panelists receive an email. The system logs "email sent." This is also accurate. But "sent" is not "read" or "understood" or "acted on." Another local success hiding the next breakdown. Layer 3: Human confirmation. A panelist receives the scorecard request and actually commits to providing feedback. This never gets logged automatically. It stays invisible. The workflow has no way to know whether "notified" translated to "committed." Layer 4: Actual outcome. The panelist submits the scorecard. This is the only signal that matters for hiring momentum—but it's also the one most likely to fail silently because it depends entirely on a human decision made outside the system. Each layer reports success locally while remaining blind to what happened in the next layer. The workflow executed. The notification delivered. The assignment logged. But did the panelist actually show up? Did they actually score? The workflow can't answer these questions because it was designed to execute, not to verify outcomes across the human boundary. By the time someone manually checks and discovers the gap, hours or days have passed. The candidate is frustrated. The round is effectively stalled. The hiring manager is confused about next steps. And the workflow still reports green. This pattern isn't unique to hiring. It's identical in any automation that depends on human follow-through—LLM agents coordinating approvals, n8n workflows triggering notifications, Zapier automations connecting systems that require human action to complete the chain. The workflow succeeds. The system succeeds. The outcome silently fails. Why This Matters at Scale Detection blindness doesn't cost much when it happens once. When a hiring round stalls, you eventually notice. A candidate withdraws. A hiring manager calls. The problem surfaces. But what happens when detection latency compounds across multiple rounds? A company running five concurrent hiring rounds, each with three panelists, each stalling at a different point in the process, creates a detection nightmare. By the time you manually check round one, rounds two through five are accumulating their own stalls. Detection lag multiplies. Coordination friction becomes invisible paralysis. Candidates drop. Hiring cycles restart. The cost of that initial detection blindness—the gap between "system said it worked" and "someone actually verified it did"—spreads downstream in ways that are hard to quantify but impossible to ignore. The same principle applies to LLM agents coordinating approvals, or to data pipelines where zero-output runs stay invisible until someone notices the report is empty. Detection blindness at the execution layer creates operational risk at the outcome layer. The longer the blindness lasts, the more cascading failures compound. What Closes the Gap The builders who avoid this trap do one thing consistently: they define success before they build. Not "the workflow ran," but "the workflow ran and the panelist actually submitted their scorecard. " Not "the agent executed," but "the agent executed and the approver actually confirmed the decision. " Not "the notification sent," but "the notification sent and the recipient actually acted on it. " This sounds obvious when you say it out loud. But most builders ship without ever writing it down. They instrument for execution success—because that's what the platform measures—and then get blindsided when execution success doesn't translate to outcome success. The fix isn't a new tool. It's a decision made upfront: What counts as success for this workflow? What are the silent-failure modes—the ways it can succeed locally while failing at the outcome layer? What verifications must you put in place before you deploy? Once you've answered these questions, the instrumentation follows naturally. You start checking whether the panelist actually showed up, not just whether the notification was sent. You start verifying whether the approver actually confirmed, not just whether the request was logged. You start measuring the gap between "workflow executed" and "outcome landed"—and you catch the cascade before it compounds. This is where the real work of reliability begins. Not in monitoring what already happened, but in thinking through what could go silently wrong before you ship. Because by the time you detect a failure, the blindness has already cost you. The lesson: Success at one layer doesn't guarantee success at the next. A workflow that reports perfect execution while producing zero real outcome is the norm, not the exception. Close the gap between "the system succeeded" and "the outcome actually landed" before you deploy—because once you're live, detection blindness cascades into operational risk faster than you can see it coming.

The same principle applies to LLM agents coordinating approvals, or to data pipelines where zero-output runs stay invisible until someone notices the report is empty. Detection blindness at the execution layer creates operational risk at the outcome layer. The longer the blindness lasts, the more cascading failures compound.

What Closes the Gap

The builders who avoid this trap do one thing consistently: they define success before they build.

Not "the workflow ran," but "the workflow ran and the panelist actually submitted their scorecard."

Not "the agent executed," but "the agent executed and the approver actually confirmed the decision."

Not "the notification sent," but "the notification sent and the recipient actually acted on it."

This sounds obvious when you say it out loud. But most builders ship without ever writing it down. They instrument for execution success—because that's what the platform measures—and then get blindsided when execution success doesn't translate to outcome success.

The fix isn't a new tool. It's a decision made upfront: What counts as success for this workflow? What are the silent-failure modes—the ways it can succeed locally while failing at the outcome layer? What verifications must you put in place before you deploy?

Once you've answered these questions, the instrumentation follows naturally. You start checking whether the panelist actually showed up, not just whether the notification was sent. You start verifying whether the approver actually confirmed, not just whether the request was logged. You start measuring the gap between "workflow executed" and "outcome landed"—and you catch the cascade before it compounds.

This is where the real work of reliability begins. Not in monitoring what already happened, but in thinking through what could go silently wrong before you ship. Because by the time you detect a failure, the blindness has already cost you.

The lesson: Success at one layer doesn't guarantee success at the next. A workflow that reports perfect execution while producing zero real outcome is the norm, not the exception. Close the gap between "the system succeeded" and "the outcome actually landed" before you deploy—because once you're live, detection blindness cascades into operational risk faster than you can see it coming.

items.title: Microsoft Teams Adds AI Phishing Detection for External Chats Starting in Early November
items.summary: Microsoft will start rolling out AI-powered, context-aware phishing detection in Microsoft Teams in early November 2026, according to a Microsoft 365 Message Center update (MC1519866) published on Wednesday. The protection targets higher-risk conversations, with external first-contact chats as the main focus for most users, and IT administrators do not need to take any action to enable it. The rollout starts with a targeted release phase that Microsoft expects to finish by mid-November. General availability worldwide is expected between early and mid-December 2026. How Teams Phishing Detection Analyzes Conversations Microsoft says the feature is meant "to help identify phishing, social engineering, impersonation attempts, and deceptive intent." Classic filters look for known indicators such as malicious links or attached files. The new Teams capability analyzes the context of a conversation instead, which lets it flag suspicious behavior in messages that contain neither. This is relevant for chat-based social engineering, where an attacker may never send a link at all. A message from an unknown external contact can now be judged on its intent rather than on its attachments. The capability first appeared in a Microsoft 365 Roadmap entry last week. The Message Center post adds the rollout schedule and the data handling commitments. Privacy Limits and What Administrators Should Expect Microsoft states that the detection system does not keep message content for later use. "This capability is used only for security protection and not for productivity, summarization, advertising, user monitoring, or other non-security purposes," the company said. "Customer message content is not retained by the detection system for model training or other secondary uses." Because the protection is enabled automatically, organizations have little to configure. Admins who want to prepare can still do the following: Track MC1519866 in the Microsoft 365 Message Center to see when the targeted release reaches the tenant. Tell help desk staff and employees that Teams may start flagging external first-contact chats as suspicious from November. Review who in the organization regularly receives first contact from external Teams users, since those chats are the main focus of the new detection. The phishing detection is the newest entry in a run of Teams security changes. Microsoft previously said admins could block external users through the Defender portal, and in August it began rolling out a meeting protection policy that automatically blocks identified external bots from joining meetings. Last month, the company said Teams will blur QR codes sent by external senders and let users report suspicious guest invitations directly in the app. In early October, Microsoft announced support for third-party deepfake detection and impersonation protection in Teams meetings. Microsoft has not said whether the context-aware detection will expand beyond higher-risk scenarios such as external first-contact chats, or whether admins will get settings to tune it once it reaches general availability in December. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.
